headline: MassHealth coverage changes reach 7,300 immigrants in Massachusetts
dek: A federal eligibility change taking effect Oct. 1 moves some lawfully present immigrants from full MassHealth coverage to narrower programs, while others remain eligible for comprehensive care.
body: A federal eligibility change took effect Thursday for about 7,300 Massachusetts residents who are lawfully present immigrants and receive MassHealth, the state’s Medicaid program. The change does not apply to U.S. citizens or nationals, and it does not end coverage for every immigrant in the affected legal categories. It changes which federal and state-funded coverage programs are available to particular members based on immigration status, age, pregnancy, disability and other eligibility factors, according to the [MassHealth information page](https://www.mass.gov/info-details/masshealth-information-for-noncitizens) and a September eligibility memo to state staff.

The affected groups can include refugees, people granted asylum, some humanitarian parolees, certain survivors of abuse or trafficking and other categories that federal law previously treated as eligible for comprehensive Medicaid. MassHealth estimates that approximately 7,300 members are affected in Massachusetts. The [Boston Globe reported](https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/09/29/metro/masshealth-medicaid-immigrants-refugees/) that more than 8,000 additional people in Connecticut, Maine, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont are expected to lose comprehensive coverage in the same federal change, putting the Massachusetts shift inside a wider New England disruption.

The practical result will not be identical for everyone. Children younger than 21 and people who are pregnant or postpartum generally keep their prior comprehensive coverage under the state’s guidance. Older adults and disabled adults who meet income and asset rules can generally move to MassHealth Family Assistance, which continues to provide comprehensive coverage but has different program rules. Some other adults will move to MassHealth Limited and the Health Safety Net, programs that can help pay for emergency services or medically necessary care at participating hospitals and community health centers but do not replace the full range of MassHealth Standard benefits.

The [GBH report](https://www.wgbh.org/news/local/2026-09-21/health-advocates-warn-of-masshealth-changes-for-immigrants-coming-oct-1) described the change as a loss of full Standard or Care Plus coverage for certain immigrants. Health advocates told GBH that some members will be moved to Family Assistance while others will have only MassHealth Limited and Health Safety Net coverage. The distinction matters at the point of care: a narrower program may help with an emergency or a qualifying visit without covering routine primary care, most prescriptions, dental care, vision care or long-term services in the same way as comprehensive coverage.

MassHealth and community organizations have been notifying members in stages. Health Care for All told GBH that notices went to roughly 2,000 people in June and more than 5,000 in July and August, followed by final notices explaining the member’s new status and appeal rights. The state’s public guidance says affected members should review their notices, respond to requests for information and use the state’s screening and assistance resources rather than assume that an immigration-status change affects everyone in the same way.

The change is likely to be felt most heavily in the state’s immigrant-serving health and social-service networks. Health Care for All identified Suffolk, Middlesex, Essex and Worcester counties as having the largest shares of affected immigrants covered through ConnectorCare, with Spanish, Brazilian Portuguese, Haitian Creole, Chinese and Russian among the languages spoken by people receiving outreach. Those county and language figures describe where advocates expect communication needs, not a count of every affected MassHealth member.

The immediate coverage change also arrives before a second phase of federal Medicaid changes. MassHealth says some adults ages 19 through 64 will face new work or education reporting requirements and more frequent renewals beginning in January 2027. Massachusetts has launched a statewide campaign with Health Care for All and community organizations to help members understand those rules, but the state must implement the federal requirements while trying to limit avoidable coverage losses.

For Massachusetts residents, the next step is individual rather than political: check the notice from MassHealth, confirm which program is listed, and ask for help if the decision appears to overlook age, pregnancy, disability, income or immigration documents. The state’s published rules make clear that being lawfully present is not itself a guarantee of one particular MassHealth category, but neither does the Oct. 1 change mean that all immigrants lose health coverage. The outcome depends on the member’s full eligibility record and on whether the person uses the appeal process when the state’s determination is disputed.
author: NorthEast News Desk
seoTitle: MassHealth changes coverage for 7,300 immigrants in Massachusetts
seoDescription: A federal eligibility change affects about 7,300 lawfully present immigrants in Massachusetts as some move from full MassHealth coverage to narrower programs.
